expectedText:
PAYMENT OF A DECEASED EMPLOYEE'S WAGES TO A SURVIVING SPOUSE WITHOUT PROBATE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Re: Payment of a Deceased Employee's Wages Without Full Probate — Pat Morgan

This information sheet describes California Probate Code §§ 13600-13606, a statutory procedure that allows Acme, Inc., as an employer, to pay salary or other compensation owed to Pat Morgan, a deceased employee, directly to Taylor Morgan -- as Pat Morgan's surviving spouse, or the guardian or conservator of the surviving spouse's estate -- without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of Pat Morgan's will. Pat Morgan died on March 15, 2026. This document is a companion to, and does not repeat, this document set's separate Unclaimed Final Wages information sheet, which addresses the different scenario where final wages cannot be delivered and eventually escheat to the state under the Unclaimed Property Law; this document instead addresses the affirmative scenario where the employer has been notified of the employee's death and a person entitled under Probate Code §§ 13600-13606 presents a declaration to collect the wages directly. This information sheet states facts about what the statute requires and permits; it does not determine that Taylor Morgan is, in fact, entitled to collect these particular wages, and it does not tell Acme, Inc. what to do about this specific unpaid amount.

THE CORE AUTHORIZATION: COLLECTING A DECEASED SPOUSE'S COMPENSATION WITHOUT PROBATE
Probate Code Chapter 4 of the statutes governing passage of property to a surviving spouse without administration -- titled "Collection by Affidavit of Compensation Owed to Deceased Spouse" -- authorizes the surviving spouse of a deceased employee, or the guardian or conservator of that surviving spouse's estate, to collect salary or other compensation an employer owes for the deceased spouse's personal services, including compensation for unused vacation, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of the will. This may be done "at any time after a spouse dies" -- the statute states no waiting period comparable to the 40-day wait that applies to some other small-estate procedures. The amount collectible this way is capped, net, and the statute's own dollar figure is periodically adjusted under a separate Probate Code provision (§ 890) every three years, each April 1, based on a Consumer Price Index formula; the Judicial Council publishes the current adjusted figure. As adjusted, the cap under §§ 13600 and 13601 is $16,625 for a decedent who died before April 1, 2022; $18,450 for a death on or after April 1, 2022 and before April 1, 2025; and $20,875 for a death on or after April 1, 2025, with the next scheduled adjustment on April 1, 2028. Currently identified unpaid compensation for Pat Morgan, according to Acme, Inc.'s records, is $3,200.00.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "At any time after a spouse dies, the surviving spouse or the guardian or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse may, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of the will, collect salary or other compensation owed by an employer for personal services of the deceased spouse, including compensation for unused vacation, not in excess of sixteen thousand six hundred twenty-five dollars ($16,625), as adjusted periodically in accordance with Section 890, net."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13600, subd. (a), Cal. Prob. Code § 13600, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13600.)
  "§§ 13600, 13601 $16,625 $18,450 $20,875"
  — Judicial Council of California, Maximum Amounts for Determining Eligibility for Summary Succession Procedures, Judicial Council of California, Maximum Amounts for Determining Eligibility for Summary Succession Procedures (adjusted amounts under Prob. Code § 890) (https://courts.ca.gov/system/files/file/probate-code-890-adjusted-amounts.pdf)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the procedure's scope, its lack of a stated waiting period, and its dollar cap mechanism -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount, and not a claim that the surviving spouse at issue qualifies as the statutory surviving spouse or that this specific amount falls within the current cap. This chapter, by its own text and the title of the Part it sits within ("Passage of Property to Surviving Spouse Without Administration"), is limited to a surviving spouse (or that spouse's guardian or conservator) collecting a deceased spouse's own compensation -- it does not name, and this document does not extend it to, other successors or an order of priority among multiple claimants, unlike the separate small-estate personal-property affidavit procedure elsewhere in the Probate Code (§ 13100 et seq.), which does list an order of priority among successors generally. The two citations below come from genuinely independent sources: the statutory text itself (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) and a Judicial Council publication (courts.ca.gov) reporting the currently adjusted dollar figures under the separate CPI-adjustment mechanism in § 890; they were fetched independently and are not subsections of the same document. This document did not independently verify whether registered domestic partners are treated as a "surviving spouse" for purposes of this chapter and does not address that question.

WHAT THE DECLARATION MUST STATE
To collect compensation under this chapter, the statute requires that an affidavit or a declaration under penalty of perjury be furnished to the employer stating specified content, including: the decedent's name; the date and place of the decedent's death; a statement identifying the affiant or declarant as either the surviving spouse or the guardian or conservator of the surviving spouse's estate; a statement that the surviving spouse is entitled to the decedent's earnings under the decedent's will or by intestate succession and that no one else has a superior right to them; and a statement that no proceeding is being or has been conducted in California for administration of the decedent's estate. The declaration must also state the statutory dollar cap and any amount already collected from other employers, and must close with a declaration that the statements are true and correct under penalty of perjury under the laws of California. The employer must also be given reasonable proof of the identity of the surviving spouse (and, where applicable, reasonable proof of a guardian's or conservator's appointment).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "an affidavit or a declaration under penalty of perjury under the laws of this state shall be furnished to the employer of the deceased spouse stating all of the following: (1) The name of the decedent. (2) The date and place of the decedent’s death. (3) Either of the following, as appropriate: (A) “The affiant or declarant is the surviving spouse of the decedent.” (B) “The affiant or declarant is the guardian or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse of the decedent.” (4) “The surviving spouse of the decedent is entitled to the earnings of the decedent under the decedent’s will or by intestate succession and no one else has a superior right to the earnings.” (5) “No proceeding is now being or has been conducted in California for administration of the decedent’s estate.”"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13601, subd. (a), Cal. Prob. Code § 13601, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13601.)
  "“The affiant or declarant affirms or declares under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.”"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13601, subd. (a)(10), Cal. Prob. Code § 13601, subd. (a)(10) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13601.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the declaration's required statutory content -- not a claim that any particular declaration submitted to the employer does, or does not, satisfy these requirements. Both citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (§ 13601) and are not independent of one another. This document quotes the required identity-proof and appointment-proof language only in summary form and does not separately verify the cross-referenced identity-proof standard in § 13104, which this research did not investigate further.

THE EMPLOYER'S DUTY TO PAY PROMPTLY ONCE THE DECLARATION IS PRESENTED
If the statutory requirements are satisfied, the employer to whom the affidavit or declaration is presented must promptly pay the decedent's earnings, including compensation for unused vacation, up to the applicable statutory cap, to the person who presented it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If the requirements of Section 13600 are satisfied, the employer to whom the affidavit or declaration is presented shall promptly pay the earnings of the decedent, including compensation for unused vacation, as provided in Section 13600, to the person presenting the affidavit or declaration."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13602, Cal. Prob. Code § 13602 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13602.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the employer's payment duty once a conforming declaration is presented -- not a claim that any specific declaration presented to the employer does, in fact, satisfy the statutory requirements referenced in it. This is a single statutory section (§ 13602); no additional independent source was located for this specific point.

THE EMPLOYER'S DISCHARGE FROM LIABILITY FOR GOOD-FAITH RELIANCE
The statute gives the employer a specific protection: if the requirements for the declaration are satisfied, the employer's receipt of the affidavit or declaration is sufficient acquittance for the compensation paid and discharges the employer from any further liability with respect to that payment. The employer may rely in good faith on the statements in the affidavit or declaration and has no duty to inquire into the truth of any statement in it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If the requirements of Section 13601 are satisfied, receipt by the employer of the affidavit or declaration constitutes sufficient acquittance for the compensation paid pursuant to this chapter and discharges the employer from any further liability with respect to the compensation paid. The employer may rely in good faith on the statements in the affidavit or declaration and has no duty to inquire into the truth of any statement in the affidavit or declaration."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13603, Cal. Prob. Code § 13603 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13603.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the discharge-from-liability rule that applies to an employer paying in good-faith reliance on a conforming declaration -- not a claim that this discharge has, in fact, been triggered for any specific payment the employer has made or is considering. This is a single statutory section (§ 13603); no additional independent source was located for this specific point.

CONSEQUENCES IF THE EMPLOYER REFUSES TO PAY
The statute also addresses the other side of the transaction: if the employer refuses to pay as the chapter requires, the surviving spouse may bring an action against the employer to recover the amount the surviving spouse is entitled to receive under the chapter, and the court must award reasonable attorney's fees to the surviving spouse if it finds the employer acted unreasonably in refusing to pay.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) If the employer refuses to pay as required by this chapter, the surviving spouse may recover the amount the surviving spouse is entitled to receive under this chapter in an action brought for that purpose against the employer. (b) If an action is brought against the employer under this section, the court shall award reasonable attorney’s fees to the surviving spouse if the court finds that the employer acted unreasonably in refusing to pay as required by this chapter."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13604, subds. (a)-(b), Cal. Prob. Code § 13604, subds. (a)-(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13604.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the remedy and fee-shifting rule that apply to an employer's refusal to pay under this chapter -- not a claim about whether any refusal by the employer would be found reasonable or unreasonable, and not a claim that any such refusal has occurred. This is a single statutory section (§ 13604, subds. (a)-(b)); no additional independent source was located for this specific point.

THIS PROCEDURE DOES NOT PRECLUDE PROBATE, AND THE RECIPIENT REMAINS ACCOUNTABLE
The statute limits what this procedure accomplishes in two ways. First, nothing in the chapter limits the rights of the deceased spouse's heirs or devisees, and payment under the chapter does not preclude later proceedings for administration of the decedent's estate -- collecting compensation this way does not close off probate. Second, the person to whom payment is made remains answerable and accountable for it to the decedent's personal representative and is liable for the amount to any other person with a superior right to it; a person who fraudulently secures payment under the chapter is liable for three times the amount to a person with a superior right. Separately, the statute states that this affidavit/declaration procedure is cumulative: it is in addition to, and not in place of, any other method of collecting compensation owed to a decedent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Nothing in this chapter limits the rights of the heirs or devisees of the deceased spouse. Payment of a decedent’s compensation pursuant to this chapter does not preclude later proceedings for administration of the decedent’s estate."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13605, Cal. Prob. Code § 13605, subds. (a)-(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13605.)
  "The procedure provided in this chapter is in addition to, and not in lieu of, any other method of collecting compensation owed to a decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13606, Cal. Prob. Code § 13606 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13606.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that the procedure is non-exclusive and that a recipient remains accountable to the estate and to persons with superior rights -- not a claim about whether the surviving spouse at issue has, or lacks, a superior right to any specific payment. The two citations below come from two separate, independently numbered sections (§§ 13605 and 13606) and are independent of one another; the two subdivisions cited within § 13605, subds. (a) and (b), are not independent of one another.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate receipt and review of this information sheet.

Deceased employee: Pat Morgan
Date of death: March 15, 2026
Surviving spouse (or guardian/conservator of the surviving spouse's estate): Taylor Morgan
Date: _______________

Acme, Inc. certifies that this information sheet was provided in connection with a request to collect compensation owed to Pat Morgan under Probate Code §§ 13600-13606.

Company representative: _______________
Date: _______________
